place: Lamontville temporary relocation area (TRA/TEA), on the banks of the Umlazi (uMlazi) river, eThekwini (Durban), KwaZulu-Natal
relocation_year: 2022 (after the April 2022 KZN floods). Some residents had already been moved in 2008 to the eMhlabeni transit camp in Lamontville after floods washed away their homes in uMlazi.
agency: eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality (City of eThekwini)
who_was_moved: Low-income residents of informal settlements in the uMlazi / Lamontville area of south Durban who had been displaced by floods; place-level only. Language or minority group: not_found.
distance_or_position: On the riverbank (banks of the Umlazi river), per Amnesty International.
risk_known_before: yes. (1) The camp area flooded in April 2022 and was publicly described as 'low-lying near the Umlaas Canal, which is prone to flooding' (Mail & Guardian op-ed, 9 May 2022). (2) The Auditor-General flagged in August 2022 that 20% of the TRUs inspected were on unsuitable land (this finding covers KZN TRUs generally, not necessarily this site). (3) An IOL Daily News headline (26 Feb 2025) refers to 'previous community warnings'; the article itself returned 403, so the content of those warnings was not verified.
temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as a temporary relocation / temporary emergency accommodation area. Residents stayed about three years (2022 to Feb 2025). Some residents had been in Lamontville transit camps since 2008, about 17 years according to an IOL search snippet.
blame_framing: Weather and climate. Mayor Xaba spoke of 'unprecedented rainfall in recent years which has crippled key infrastructure like roads and bridges' (GroundUp). He also blamed land scarcity: 'We don't have enough land to settle people.' No official acceptance of responsibility for the site choice was found.
warning_at_site: The South African Weather Service issued 'a Yellow Level 2 warning for the southern parts of KZN for severe thunderstorms' (Daily Maverick). Whether the warning reached TRA residents, and in what language (e.g. isiZulu), was not found.
resident_voice: Yes, but limited in the sources accessed. Flood victims interviewed by IOL spoke mainly of looting of their belongings. An IOL headline reports a grieving mother calling for urgent relocation (not fetched).
accountability_outcome: The Amnesty International report (Nov 2025) documented the case and found a 'serious failure to ensure that flood victims are relocated to safety'. No inquiry, court case, resignation or compensation specific to the site was found.

place: Gwala Street transit camp, Lamontville, eThekwini (Durban), KwaZulu-Natal (near the Umlaas canal)
relocation_year: Feb/March 2021 (after about two years in tents at Tehuis Hostel following the April 2019 floods)
agency: eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality; residents were ordered back by the ward councillor
who_was_moved: Low-income, mostly unemployed former informal-settlement residents of Mega Village, uMlazi. Language or minority group: not_found.
distance_or_position: Low-lying ground near the Umlaas canal, above a high-voltage cable.
risk_known_before: Partly. Before the 2022 flood, Daily Maverick (23 Mar 2022) reported that Eskom officials had marked the site unsafe for habitation (electrical hazard, not flood). An assessment of flood risk before the 2021 relocation was not_found.
temporary_vs_permanent: A transit camp (temporary). Residents were in tents 2019-2021 and in the camp from 2021, and were still there in 2022.
blame_framing: Residents and dumping (paraphrase): the municipal spokesperson 'attributed flooding to illegal dumping and people building on floodplains' (Daily Maverick opinion, 2022).
resident_voice: Yes. A 47-year-old grandmother (GroundUp): 'We have been moved from one place to another and we are tired now.' Shelter occupants said they 'did not have dignified, safe accommodation' (M&G).

place: Isipingo transit camp (Willcox Road), south Durban, eThekwini, KwaZulu-Natal
relocation_year: 2009 (DA statement says 2010)
flooded_years: multiple ('four or five occasions'), including April 2022
agency: eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality
who_was_moved: Low-income informal-settlement residents from Umlazi, the Bluff and Mayville. Language or minority group: not_found.
distance_or_position: Between a river and a highway; reportedly on a flood plain.
risk_known_before: not_found (no pre-relocation assessment located)
temporary_vs_permanent: Residents were promised better houses 'after six to nine months'. More than 300 families were still there after about 13-14 years.
blame_framing: not_found
resident_voice: Yes. A camp committee member: 'On four or five occasions, we have experienced flooding and our household items have been damaged by mud and water.'
accountability_outcome: none found (protests; a political party statement)

place: Temporary residential units (TRUs) for April 2022 flood victims, KwaZulu-Natal (province-wide sample)
flooded_years: not_found (audit finding, not a flood event)
agency: KZN Department of Human Settlements and contractors (TRU programme), audited by the Auditor-General of South Africa (AGSA)
who_was_moved: Flood-displaced households across KZN, largely from informal settlements.
distance_or_position: 'unsuitable land' (not further specified in sources accessed)
risk_known_before: yes. AGSA flagged unsuitable siting in August 2022, before the February 2025 floods.
temporary_vs_permanent: Temporary. The DA estimated in October 2022 that delivery could take up to four years.
blame_framing: not_found
resident_voice: not_found
accountability_outcome: An AGSA audit and parliamentary oversight. No sanctions specific to siting were found.

place: Proposed relocation site at Cullinan (near Rayton), City of Tshwane, Gauteng, for 2022 Mamelodi flood victims (e.g. from Eerste Fabriek on the Moretele River)
relocation_year: planned (2025)
flooded_years: not_found (the site has not been reported as flooded)
agency: Gauteng Provincial Government / City of Tshwane
who_was_moved: Low-income informal-settlement residents of Mamelodi (proposed).
distance_or_position: Alleged wetland
risk_known_before: Alleged by an opposition party (DA, Mar 2025) before the relocation.
temporary_vs_permanent: not_found
blame_framing: not_found
resident_voice: Mamelodi resident (Daily Maverick, 2022): 'I live in fear whenever there is heavy rain.'

place: Cyclone Idai resettlement sites in Sofala (esp. Buzi, Dondo, Chibabava, Nhamatanda, Caia), Manica and Zambezia provinces
relocation_year: 2019 (after Cyclone Idai, March 2019) and 2019-2020 floods
agency: Government of Mozambique via INGD (National Institute for Disaster Risk Management), with IOM and humanitarian partners
who_was_moved: Rural and peri-urban cyclone survivors in central Mozambique, largely subsistence farmers (place-level).
distance_or_position: Various; several were reachable only across flood-prone roads.
risk_known_before: not_found (no pre-siting flood assessment located). The sites were presented as safe from flooding.
temporary_vs_permanent: Resettlement sites intended as permanent; many residents still lived in emergency tents nearly two years later.
blame_framing: not_found
resident_voice: Resident of a later higher-ground site (IOM): 'it is higher up and already withstood the last harsh rains and storms, and it is proven to not flood.'

place: Hopley Farm settlement (incl. Gada area), Harare
agency: Government of Zimbabwe / City of Harare (Operation Garikai/Hlalani Kuhle)
who_was_moved: Low-income urban evictees pushed out of central Harare (place-level).
distance_or_position: Part of the settlement (Gada) is in a wetland.
risk_known_before: not_found
temporary_vs_permanent: Started as temporary accommodation for evictees (2005); it became a long-term settlement (more than 17 years).
blame_framing: Denial / unawareness (see government_response).
resident_voice: Resident (GroundUp): 'I thank God no one was inside. We could be counting bodies.'
accountability_outcome: none found (UN criticism of Murambatsvina in general)

relocation_year: from 2013-2014 (conflict); flood-displaced people also moved into the camp area after 2020

place: Kannagi Nagar, Ezhil Nagar (Pallikaranai marsh) and Perumbakkam resettlement colonies, southern Chennai, Tamil Nadu
relocation_year: Early 2000s onward; big waves after the 2004 tsunami and after the December 2015 floods (2015-2023)
flooded_years: Perumbakkam: 2015, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2023 (per IRCDUC); Kannagi Nagar and Ezhil Nagar flood in routine monsoons, including 2015
agency: Government of Tamil Nadu; Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board, now the Tamil Nadu Urban Habitat Development Board (TNUHDB), which built the tenements
who_was_moved: Low-income, informal riverbank slum dwellers from inner Chennai. Down To Earth reports the affected communities are largely Dalit. Tamil-speaking.
distance_or_position: Former wetland/marsh; lake catchment; floodplain on the city's southern periphery, about 25-30 km from the original settlements
risk_known_before: Partly. It was widely known the land was marsh and lake catchment: Kannagi Nagar and Ezhil Nagar were built on the Pallikaranai marsh, a recognised wetland. We found no formal pre-relocation official risk assessment in the sources.
temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent tenements. People have stayed for decades (Kannagi Nagar since the early 2000s).
blame_framing: not_found (no official quote). Advocates frame it as state policy: evictions 'under the guise of post-flood rehabilitation' (paraphrased in search summary of HLRN / Citizen Matters).
resident_voice: A relief volunteer told The Caravan: 'People in Ezhilnagar were furious that not a single official from the government had come to visit them.'
accountability_outcome: none found (no inquiry or compensation); the draft R&R policy remains unfinalised

place: Semmencheri (Semmencherry) resettlement tenements, southern Chennai, Tamil Nadu
relocation_year: About 2005-2006 onward (post-2004 tsunami and slum clearance); 6,734 apartments
flooded_years: 2015 (16 November and 1 December), 2023 (Cyclone Michaung); residents describe five floods in eight years
agency: Tamil Nadu Slum Clearance Board (now TNUHDB), Government of Tamil Nadu
who_was_moved: Low-income slum and tsunami-affected families, including fishing households. Tamil-speaking.
distance_or_position: Low-lying land near Thazhambur lake on the southern periphery, about 30 km from central Chennai
risk_known_before: not_found (no pre-2015 official warning found)
temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent tenements; occupied for about 20 years
blame_framing: not_found
warning_at_site: not_found. The 2015 flood hit at about 3 am as homes 'rapidly' filled, which suggests no effective warning (inference, not stated).
resident_voice: In 2023: 'Aren't we human? Didn't we cast our votes during the election? Why do they neglect us now?' and 'We were told that if they tried to reach us, their vehicles would've got stuck in the water.'

place: Corail-Cesselesse relocation camp and surrounding Canaan area, north of Port-au-Prince
relocation_year: 2010 (camp opened 22 March 2010; families moved from a Port-au-Prince IDP camp in April 2010)
flooded_years: Assessed as flooding 'regularly at least once a year' (IOM, July 2010). Storms and wind damaged tents in July 2010; the camp was evacuated before Hurricane Tomas in November 2010.
agency: Government of Haiti (site selection under strong pressure from the international community and U.S. military); camp built and run by World Vision, IOM and the American Refugee Committee
who_was_moved: Earthquake-displaced, very low-income, informal-camp residents from Port-au-Prince. Haitian Creole-speaking.
distance_or_position: Barren plain at the foot of hills, prone to sheet flooding and wind, about 15 km north of Port-au-Prince
risk_known_before: Yes, before permanent build-out: IOM flagged it in writing on 29 July 2010, after the first relocations (March-April 2010) but before later shelter construction. It was not flagged before the first move.
temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as a temporary planned relocation camp with 'transitional shelters'. It became a permanent informal city, still occupied more than a decade later.
blame_framing: Blame was shifted between actors (government vs international community vs NGO). No one was found accepting responsibility. The former mayor said: 'local authorities were ignored and almost all the decisions were made by the central government… we were not at all implicated in the choice of the site.'
warning_at_site: Before Hurricane Tomas (November 2010), a police officer at the camp shouted through a megaphone 'The hurricane is not a joke!' (search excerpt, Time). The language is not stated; Haitian Creole is likely but not confirmed.
resident_voice: 'They just dumped us here'; 'Imagine: they put you here, but there's no work' (IPS, 2013).

place: Bhasan Char island, Bay of Bengal (Noakhali district)
relocation_year: December 2020 onward (nearly 20,000 by mid-2021; about 33,800 later reported)
flooded_years: Signs of water on building balconies reported after Cyclone Amphan (May 2020). No catastrophic flood documented in the sources; the case rests on assessed risk.
agency: Government of Bangladesh (Navy built the facility with Chinese contractor Sinohydro)
who_was_moved: Stateless Rohingya refugees (Rohingya-language speakers), camp residents with no formal housing rights
distance_or_position: Low-lying silt island (char) in the Meghna estuary/Bay of Bengal, surrounded by an embankment, hours by boat from the mainland
risk_known_before: Yes. Rights groups and experts warned before and during the transfers (HRW 2019 and 2021 reports).
temporary_vs_permanent: Described by the government as a relocation facility pending repatriation to Myanmar; in practice long-term (years)
blame_framing: The government framed the move as a safety and congestion solution. No acceptance of risk was found.
resident_voice: Refugees reported 'clear signs of water on the balconies' after Cyclone Amphan (HRW).

place: Rohingya refugee camps (Kutupalong-Balukhali and others, 33 camps), Cox's Bazar
relocation_year: 2017 (mass influx; land allocated by the government on deforested hills and low ground)
agency: Government of Bangladesh (land allocation, shelter rules); camps managed with UNHCR and IOM
who_was_moved: Stateless Rohingya refugees, Rohingya-language speakers
distance_or_position: Steep cut hillsides and low valleys/paddy land
risk_known_before: Yes. Landslide and flood risk was assessed by agencies from 2018 (landslide risk studies; UNHCR/IOM relocation of at-risk families).
temporary_vs_permanent: Officially temporary; flimsy shelters are required by policy. Occupied since 2017 (9+ years).
blame_framing: Monsoon and weather framing in UN releases. HRW places responsibility on the government's shelter restrictions.
warning_at_site: not_found in fetched sources (a volunteer early-warning system exists in the camps but was not documented in these sources)
resident_voice: 'Rainwater leaks in because there are now holes in the tarpaulin roof, and the storm can easily damage the shelters within seconds.' (HRW)

place: Ashrayan-2 houses on Biramer Pachgachi Char, Sariakandi upazila, Bogura (Jamuna river)
relocation_year: 2020-2022 (houses built in fiscal 2021-22 / 2020-21)
flooded_years: 2024 (houses lost to Jamuna erosion and floodwater by October 2024). The Ashrayan project generally reports stranding in floods.
agency: Government of Bangladesh, Ashrayan-2 project (Prime Minister's Office; district and upazila administration)
who_was_moved: Landless, homeless and very poor rural char dwellers. Bangla-speaking.
distance_or_position: On an eroding riverbank of an active char in the Jamuna; within the legal 50-yard setback
risk_known_before: Yes. According to The Daily Star, the relevant officials 'always advise the district administration not to construct any paved or semi-paved infrastructure in the char areas'; the 50-yard legal setback also existed.
temporary_vs_permanent: Announced as permanent homes (semi-pucca). Some were lost within about 2-3 years.
blame_framing: River erosion and nature framing; officials deflected. No acceptance of responsibility was found.
resident_voice: 'Now the houses given by the government are also going.' 'We have to leave this char again and take shelter in another char, as the river erosion is taking a dangerous turn.'

place: Kasiglahan Village (NHA resettlement), Barangay San Jose, Rodriguez (Montalban), Rizal
relocation_year: 1999-2000 (Pasig River evictees); expanded after Ondoy in 2009-2010, including new units built on the flooded Phase 1K in 2010
agency: National Housing Authority (NHA), with the developer New San Jose Builders
who_was_moved: Low-income informal settler families evicted from Metro Manila waterways and danger zones. Filipino/Tagalog-speaking.
distance_or_position: Montalban River floodplain, former rice paddies, downstream of Wawa Dam; also near the Marikina fault
risk_known_before: Yes, before the later phases: Ondoy (2009) flooded the site before new units went up in 2010, and the LGU declared a danger zone in 2012, before Ulysses in 2020.
temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent resettlement; occupied for about 25 years
blame_framing: The NHA cited budget constraints. Residents blamed dam releases made without warning. Activists (alleged) questioned the NHA-developer contracts.
warning_at_site: No. Residents said the Wawa Dam released water without prior notice in 2009 (Bulatlat). The Montalban Relocatees Alliance demanded an early-warning system.
resident_voice: 'The waters rose very quickly, unlike the ones before. We were not able to bring anything, not even extra clothes.' 'After Ulysses, people here get anxious every time it rains.'
accountability_outcome: none found. Activists called for an investigation of the NHA and New San Jose Builders contracts (alleged irregularities, not established).

place: Tzu Chi Great Love Village (Tzu Chi Love City), Barangay Liloan, Ormoc City, Leyte
relocation_year: About 2014-2016 (post-Typhoon Haiyan/Yolanda); about 1,565 families
agency: Tzu Chi Foundation (NGO) in partnership with Ormoc City government (land/beneficiary side) – the government role is not fully confirmed in fetched sources
who_was_moved: Low-income typhoon survivors, many from informal coastal settlements. Waray/Cebuano-speaking region.
distance_or_position: Low-lying portion (Block 20) of an inland resettlement site
risk_known_before: not_found
temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent village; about 10+ years
blame_framing: not_found
resident_voice: not_found

place: Arbor Court Apartments, 802 Seminar, Greens Bayou, Houston, Texas
relocation_year: HUD project-based Section 8 subsidies from 1991 (placement of low-income tenants, not disaster relocation)
flooded_years: 2016 (Tax Day flood), 2017 (Hurricane Harvey); also reported earlier
agency: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), subsidising a private owner
who_was_moved: Very low-income, HUD-subsidised tenants. Texas Housers reports about 95% of residents are African American (complex-level statistic).
distance_or_position: In the floodway of Greens Bayou (the complex backs onto the bayou)
risk_known_before: Yes. FEMA floodplain mapping (1985) preceded the 1991 HUD subsidies (per Houston Chronicle, search excerpt).
temporary_vs_permanent: Permanent subsidised housing; tenants stayed for years
blame_framing: HUD: no comment, citing litigation
resident_voice: not_found (tenant lawsuit complaints about mould and flooding)
accountability_outcome: Federal lawsuit against HUD (2018; alleged discrimination, outcome not found). The city's refusal of a rebuild permit was upheld by a judge, per a Houston Chronicle headline.

flooded_years: July 2024 (windstorm and flash floods); July 2026 (floods damaged the Zero Point returnee compound wall)

who_was_moved: Afghan returnees and deportees from Pakistan, often destitute. Pashto/Dari-speaking.
distance_or_position: not_found (border valley; exact position vs drainage not stated)
risk_known_before: not_found
temporary_vs_permanent: Temporary transit camp
blame_framing: Weather framing (OCHA flash updates)
resident_voice: not_found

place: Relocation site in Kohod village, Tangerang regency (near the PIK2 development), Banten

risk_known_before: not_found
temporary_vs_permanent: not_found

resident_voice: 'This used to be rice field. Now it's a relocation site.' 'We don't mind having to be relocated, but please give us proper facilities that are safe and don't flood.'
